Think tank Phoenix Insights rebrands under Standard Life
Phoenix Group’s think-tank, Phoenix Insights, has rebranded as the Standard Life Centre for the Future of Retirement.
Since its inception in 2021, the firm said Phoenix Insights has been active in driving action for some of the biggest challenges of people living longer.
It listed actions such as influencing policymakers’ thinking on pensions adequacy and economic inactivity and building partnerships to promote the untapped potential of workers in their 50s and 60s.
With more than half of all defined contribution pension savers retiring between 2025 and 2060 expected to be either not saving enough for retirement, Phoenix said its think-tank will focus on how society can achieve financial security for all in later life.
Catherine Foot, director of the Standard Life Centre for the Future for Retirement, said: “How we work, save, and retire is changing. That traditional idea of spending decades in full-time employment and then retiring with a comfortable, guaranteed income is no longer going to be a reality for most people.
“There is an under-saving crisis in the UK, and if we don’t act now, we risk millions reaching retirement unable to afford the standard of living they expect.”
Foot said she was “incredibly proud” of what has been achieved under Phoenix Insights, and said working under the Standard Life brand will “supercharge” its ability to further raise awareness.
“This is particularly important at present following the government’s expected review of retirement adequacy which provides a critical opportunity to reshape our pensions system to better address some of the challenges future retirees are facing,” she added.
The Standard Life Centre for the Future of Retirement will campaign for future generations of retirees to:
Be included in sufficient and affordable private pension saving ​
Be supported to make good decisions throughout life about their pension saving and retirement income ​
Work in good quality, flexible jobs that suit their lives, and able to actively manage their careers​
Be protected from poverty with state support through an adequate and sustainable State Pension and benefits system
Andy Briggs, CEO at Phoenix Group, said: “Standard Life has sought to act as a force for good and to champion the needs of everyday people for over two hundred years.
“And as the engine behind Phoenix’s Group’s 12mn customers, it is in prime position to speak about the challenges everyone faces when it comes to how we work, save and plan for retirement.
“The addition of the pioneering think-tank is both a celebration of the milestone and a statement of intent about the brand’s ongoing desire to act as source of innovation and practical support to customers and society alike.”
The Standard Life Centre for the Future of Retirement will launch its first report in June looking at the impact of the government’s industrial strategy on different sectors of the UK workforce.
It will also explore the potential impact of the FCA’s proposed introduction of targeted support for savers over 45 in July.

Standard Life builds momentum in workplace pensions
Tom Browne 16 March 2026
Standard Life reported continued growth across its pensions and retirement businesses in 2025, with strong workplace inflows, rising annuity sales and significant pension risk transfer activity.
In its full-year results, the provider said its Workplace division delivered net inflows of £5.3bn during the year, unchanged from 2024, supported by £10bn in gross inflows.
New workplace members increased by 14% to 247,000, taking the total number of workplace customers to three million for the first time.
Standard Life said the results reflected “continued execution across all our strategic priorities”, including a focus on customer engagement, distribution and strengthening its position in workplace pensions.
The firm added that it expects annual market flows of around £80bn in the pensions and savings market, and intends to consolidate its position as a top-three provider.
It has already secured £1bn of new wins for 2026 and reported a medium-term opportunity pipeline of more than £10bn.
Standard Life unveils ‘affordable’ pensions advice service
Group chief executive Andy Briggs said the results demonstrated “strong progress delivering on our strategic priorities”.
“Our results demonstrate strong progress delivering on our strategic priorities,” he said.
“Further profitable growth and a strengthened Solvency balance sheet have supported increased shareholder returns and greater financial flexibility for the future, underpinned by the significant and growing levels of excess cash our business generates.
“We are firmly on track to deliver our 2026 financial targets, building momentum by continuing to sharpen our competitive position in one of the world’s most attractive savings and retirement markets.”
Briggs also pointed to the continued momentum of the firm’s workplace proposition.
“Our Workplace business continued its strong momentum in 2025, delivering net fund flows of £5.3bn,” he said.
“This is a structurally growing market, and the investment we’ve made in our offer in recent years is paying off. New business and retention remained strong, and our total Workplace customer base reached three million for the first time.”
In retirement solutions, Standard Life reported £1.2bn in individual annuity premiums written during 2025, up from £1bn the previous year, with market share increasing to 15%.
Briggs said demand had been supported by the appeal of guaranteed retirement income.
“Individual annuity sales also grew for the third consecutive year since re-entering the market, supported by customer demand for income certainty and attractive rates.”
The company also completed £3.9bn of pension risk transfer transactions during the year, including its largest ever deal valued at £1.9bn.
“The performance reflects the continued confidence from trustees and sponsors in our employer proposition, excellent member experience and competitive pricing,” Briggs said.
Looking ahead, he said 2026 could prove significant for the pensions sector as a series of policy initiatives take shape.
“The Pension Schemes Bill will lay the foundations for a move to fewer, larger workplace schemes and creates the potential for greater value for money,” he said.
He added that the upcoming interim report from the Pensions Commission would provide an opportunity to address under-saving.
“This is a once in a generation opportunity to ensure we tackle current levels of under-saving and help people to engage with their financial futures.”

Standard Life workplace net inflows hit £5.3bn
Firm’s full-year results reveal new workplace members were up 14% in 2025
Standard Life has published its full year results for 2025.
The provider revealed workplace net inflows during 2025 reached £5.3bn, remaining the same as the previous year, with gross inflows up to £10bn from £9.3bn in 2024.

Standard Life reports steady growth and rising annuity demand
Hereward Mills Growth in Standard Life’s workplace pension business remained steady in 2025, its annual report has revealed.

According to the 23-page results document, net inflows for workplace pensions remained at £5.3bn, the same level as in 2024.
That was despite gross inflows increasing to £10bn, up from £9.3bn in 2024, indicating higher withdrawals in 2025.
However, new workplace members grew by 14 per cent to 247,000 in 2025, bringing the total to 3mn.
Andy Briggs, group chief executive at Standard Life, said: “This is a structurally growing market, and the investment we’ve made in our offering in recent years is paying off.
“New business and retention remained strong, and our total workplace customer base reached three million for the first time.”
Elsewhere, the value of annuity premiums written rose to £1.2bn, up from £1bn in 2024, to a market share of 15 per cent.
Briggs said: “Individual annuity sales also grew for the third consecutive year since re-entering the market, supported by customer demand for income certainty and attractive rates.”
The volume of pension risk transfers decreased to £3.9bn, down from £5.1bn in 2024, despite Standard Life’s largest ever deal at £1.9bn.
Briggs says it has been a good start for the Pension Risk Transfer business, in 2026 “with an additional £1.6bn of transactions completed or at an exclusive stage.”
Overall, Briggs is excited about 2026, welcoming change in the pensions and savings industry.
“The pension schemes bill will lay the foundations for a move to fewer, larger workplace schemes and creates the potential for greater value for money.
“We are expecting an interim report from the Pension Commission in the coming months which will set out the challenge society collectively needs to address under-saving.
“This is a once in a generation opportunity to ensure we tackle current levels of under-saving and help people to engage with their financial futures.”

Standard Life aims to tackle £8bn outflows with advice proposition
The net outflow figure of £7.8bn is down from £8.6bn in 2024 reflecting ‘retail strategy green shoots’.
Standard Life saw net outflows of £7.8bn in its retail business, but aims to tackle these losses with its newly launched flat-fee advice service.
In its full year results for 2025, the insurer revealed gross inflows for its retail proposition of £7.1bn. The net outflow figure of £7.8bn is down from £8.6bn in 2024 reflecting ‘retail strategy green shoots’.
In October last year, Standard Life launched a flat-fee advice service that will charge clients £1,000 for advice on their pensions. The service is pitched at clients approaching retirement with at least £50,000 in defined contribution pension savings.
Like other providers such as Aviva, who have also launched similar services, Standard Life is seeking to offer advice and targeted support to its pension customers, in order to stop them moving to other providers when they retire.
‘Alongside our newly launched advice proposition, targeted support will enhance our ability to offer timely services to our customers and is very much aligned to our belief that everyone’s journey to and through retirement can be better,’ the group said.
Under CEO Andy Briggs, the strategy at Standard Life represents a shift from being a ‘closed-book consolidator’, to an open growth business focused on workplace and retirement.
In late 2023, Briggs re-entered the individual annuity market.
According to the results, individual annuity sales grew for the third consecutive year since the re-entry, supported by demand for income certainty and high interest rates. The business wrote £1.2bn of premiums and increased its market share to 15% from 8% two years ago.
Standard Life officially rebranded to Standard Life PLC last week as it seeks to make the brand ‘more relevant for more people’.
The results detailed its technology transformation of its operating model with the continuation of its migration to outsourcers TCS Diligenta and Wipro. Standard Life said 75% of its policies are now on new platforms, up from 45% in 2024.

Standard Life launches brand awareness campaign as Phoenix Group switches name
Standard Life has launched a campaign to strengthen its brand as Phoenix Group Holdings completes its name change to Standard Life.
The campaign, ‘For the life we live’, will run for 10 weeks across TV, radio, newsprint, digital, and social media and will aim to increase brand awareness.
It will also contribute to Standard Life achieving its new target of helping three million more customers over the next 10 years to take action towards a better retirement.
Standard Life CEO, Andy Briggs, said: “For more than 200 years, Standard Life has stood beside its customers, helping them plan and prepare for their long-term financial futures.
“Today, as Standard Life plc, we are proud to manage £300bn in assets on behalf of 12 million customers.
“Our purpose is helping people secure a life of possibilities, and I am proud to announce our new target, which embodies our belief that everyone’s journey to and through retirement can be better.”
The launch of the campaign coincides with the retirement specialist officially changing its name from Phoenix Group to Standard Life.
As a result, the specialist will be listed on the London Stock Exchange under the ticker of SDLF from today (March 2nd).

The change recognises the progress made in recent years by Phoenix Group to simplify the business.
Customer brands within the group, including SunLife, Phoenix Life, and ReAssure, will continue to invest in customer service and operate as normal.
“The move to Standard Life supports our vision to be the UK’s leading retirement savings and income business, and demonstrates our commitment to helping customers achieve better outcomes and greater financial security in later life,” Briggs added.
“We want Standard Life to be the business that people trust to guide their retirement journey.”

Phoenix Group Holdings plc completes its name change to Standard Life plc
Standard Life plc (‘Standard Life’ or the ‘Group’), a retirement specialist focused entirely on retirement saving and income, has completed its name change from Phoenix Group Holdings plc (‘Phoenix Group’) and will be listed on the London Stock Exchange under the ticker of SDLF from 8am today.
The move to Standard Life plc supports the organic growth strategy of the Pensions and Savings and Retirement Solutions businesses that already trade under the Standard Life brand. Since Phoenix Group bought the brand, it has built leading positions in a number of markets including workplace pensions, individual annuities and pension risk transfer.
Standard Life champions the belief that everyone’s journey to and through retirement can be better. For more than 200 years, Standard Life has been standing beside its customers, to help them plan and prepare for their financial futures.
The change to Standard Life plc recognises the progress made in recent years by Phoenix Group to simplify the business and enables the Group’s vision to be the UK’s leading retirement savings and income business.
The Group will continue to lead the industry, by advocating for better retirements and convening to drive meaningful change to help customers achieve greater financial security.
To mark this change, Standard Life has set a new target to help three million more customers over the next ten years take action towards a better retirement. To meet this commitment, the Group will provide support and solutions designed to ensure more people are on track for sufficient pension savings and more people are financially secure in later life. Standard Life will evidence this by tracking improvement in two customer outcomes:  more people are engaged in planning for their retirement, and more people are supported to make better decisions when accessing their pension.
An extensive consumer brand campaign ‘For the life we live’ has also been launched – a national multi-media campaign featuring TV, radio, newsprint, digital and social advertising. It will run for ten weeks with the aim of strengthening the Standard Life brand at key customer decision points in people’s journey to and through retirement and helping inspire customers to engage with their financial futures.
Customer brands within the Group, including SunLife, Phoenix Life and ReAssure, will continue to invest in customer service and operate as normal. This move will see no change as part of the structure of the Group, or the legal entity.

We can save people from having poor retirements. Here’s how
Andy Briggs has changed insurer Phoenix’s name to Standard Life. He says only one in seven people are saving enough for old age
This weekend, he’s raising his voice for another reason: he wants the City to know about his decision to change the name of Phoenix, the FTSE 100 insurer he has run for six years, to Standard Life.
“We’re a purpose-led, consumer-orientated retirement savings business,” the 59-year-old says earnestly. “It better describes that.”
The move means that Standard Life is once again on the stock market nine years after its £11 billion tie-up with rival Aberdeen Asset Management. Phoenix has taken the name after a series of complex transactions with the FTSE 250 fund manager (Aberdeen has abandoned its own rebranding to the vowel-depleted Abrdn), which still has a 10 per cent stake in what is now Standard Life.
Briggs does not have an office of his own in the insurer’s London head office, as he prefers to sit in the open-plan space. So he usually uses a meeting room named Richmond. As he lowers his 6ft 5in frame into a chair, he explains that the room is aptly named because he spends his weekends on the golf course in the southwest London borough.
Briggs has had to put in the hours since arriving in March 2020. On his watch, Phoenix has changed from an acquisition machine — built by buying “zombie” insurance firms closed to new business — to a company aiming to sell new products under the Standard Life brand.
The business is valued at £7 billion on the stock market and manages £300 billion of assets for 12 million people. About 2,000 of the 5,000 staff are located in Edinburgh — where the old Standard Life used to be — with 700 of them in London.
Some wonder why he did not act sooner in rechristening Phoenix as Standard Life. Briggs insists it could not be rushed: “Changing the name doesn’t change the substance of the business. I wanted to get the substance in place first.”
Briggs says that he was always motivated by “leadership”. He arrived at Phoenix after missing out on the top job at FTSE 100 rival Aviva. “I played team sports as a kid and was often captain and loved the leadership side. My mates used to tease me about it, but very early on, I had this sense that management was what I wanted to do,” he explains.
Since arriving at what is now Standard Life, he has battled to bring down its leverage levels by generating £1.4 billion of cash profit — in essence, a measure of cashflow — each year.
The company’s share price endured its biggest drop for five years at the interim results in September, so Briggs will aim to reassure analysts when he presents the full-year figures next week. The City will also be looking for any update on whether he will buy the UK arm of Aegon, which is also said to be in the sights of Royal Bank of Canada, Barclays and Lloyds. “We’re having a look,” he confirms. “Whenever any business comes to market in the UK, we always have a look.”
Briggs will also be asked about progress on bringing in external partners to help buy up corporate pensions through what are known as bulk purchase annuities.
At its simplest, Briggs uses £1.1 billion of the cash profit to pay the dividend and pay down debt and is using the extra £300 million to get the debt back to the levels of his company’s rivals: “Investors have said to us, we’d like to see your leverage come down in line with peers. Once we’ve done that, from the end of this year, we’ll have that available for either additional shareholder returns or investment into growth.”
But investors have been concerned by problems implementing IFRS 17, a set of accounting rules that started in 2023 about governing insurance contracts, which led to the chief executive having £70,000 docked off his bonus last year.
The name change to Standard Life is part of Briggs’s determination to be a “champion” for people saving for their retirement.
“You can’t see [yet] that in 10, 20 years’ time, people retiring are going to have a really poor income and poor standing of living — and that’s why there needs to be a ‘champion’ to change that,” he explains. “So when we say ‘champion’, it is because consumers are not going to get the retirement they would like and expect unless something changes,” he says.
The government’s independent Pensions Commission is reviewing this and due to report next year. Briggs is clear: “I find it impossible to believe that an independent commission can possibly conclude 8 per cent is enough.” He advocates a rise to 12 per cent, in stages, which “is getting into better territory”.
Getting to retirement should also take longer, he says, citing research showing that the retirement age should rise by eight years globally if the dependency ratio — the number of people working versus those who are retired — is to remain static. So, he advocates helping the over-50s to stay in work, particularly through flexible hours: “If the over-50s fall out of work, they are the group that are by far the least likely to get back into work.”
As for young people needing jobs, he says this will come if the economy grows more rapidly. “That will create jobs for the young folk and the over-50s,” he argues.
Fuelling economic growth was one of the issues tackled by Standard Life’s chairman, Sir Nicholas Lyons, when he was lord mayor of the City three years ago. He created the first iteration of the Mansion House Accord to encourage pension funds to invest 10 per cent of their workplace schemes in private assets such as infrastructure projects by 2030.
The Association of British Insurers, where Briggs is president, stepped up its fight last week to stop the government putting in a legislative backstop to mandate this level of investment, if it is not achieved voluntarily. Briggs is also clear that “it’s really critical we track the progress”.
“The politicians and the regulators, they do their bit of legislation or regulation and think, well that’s it, done. It’s only done when you see the outcome,” he says.

Standard Life buys Aegon UK for £2bn
The deal will create a £480bn provider with 16 million customers.
Standard Life has bought Aegon’s UK business in a £2bn deal, the insurer announced this morning.
The deal will create a £480bn provider with 16 million customers.
One source said the other bidder for the business was Lloyds which offered a higher cash price, but Standard Life in the end was preferred for a cash / equity deal.
Following the deal, which brings across £180bn of assets, Standard Life will seek to expand its advice presence, with Aegon owning advice business Origen Financial Services, alongside two adviser platforms: The Aegon Platform (formerly Cofunds) and Aegon Retirement Choices.
The acquisition is part cash (£750m) and part shares, with Aegon’s Dutch parent company being given 181 million shares in Standard Life, meaning it will become a 15.3% shareholding in the provider. Aegon will be able to nominate an executive to the Standard Life board.
Aberdeen also still holds a minority stake in Standard Life and the group said Aberdeen is ‘supportive’ of the strategy and remains a committed shareholder.
Aegon, which has its own international fund management arm, Aegon Asset Management, will also become an ‘asset management partner’ for Standard Life following the deal. Aegon Asset Management is not included in the UK sale.
Speaking to analysts, Standard Life CEO Andy Briggs said Aegon Asset Management has an agreement to continue to run the £20bn of assets which it currently does for the Aegon UK book following the takeover.
Standard Life said there was an opportunity for £800m in synergies between the two groups, ‘underpinned by Standard Life’s experience in large and complex life insurance integrations’.
Aegon uses Atos to administer many of its policies, which includes many closed book divisions, and Standard Life uses Diligenta for the administration of much of its back book. In the past Standard Life, which recently changed its name from Phoenix, moved pension books onto Diligenta’s administration platform following takeovers of other life companies to strip out costs.
Aegon has a large workplace pension business, with £74bn of assets and Standard Life said the deal will see it become the second-largest player in the workplace pension market.
At the bell Standard Life’s shares were up 1.7%.
Briggs, said: ‘Our agreement to acquire Aegon UK significantly accelerates our vision to be the UK’s leading retirement savings and income business.
‘We will be in an even stronger position to meet the evolving needs of our 16 million customers with enhanced digital, advice and distribution capabilities across workplace and retail, strengthening our standing in one of the world’s most attractive markets.’
Briggs added the deal also ‘transforms our adviser offering’, which it was already building out. As well as its independent arm Origen, Aegon also acquired Nationwide’s financial planning business in 2023, which included 200 restricted financial planners.

Standard Life strikes £2bn deal to buy Aegon UK
Standard Life has agreed to buy rival Aegon’s UK business for £2 billion in a move set to create a pension and savings giant with 16 million customers and £480 million assets under administration.
The deal will see Standard Life – recently rebranded from Phoenix Group – pay £750 million in cash, part-funded through debt, and issue 181.1 million new shares to Dutch financial firm Aegon.
Aegon will own a 15.3% stake in FTSE 100 listed Standard Life following the acquisition and can appoint one non-executive director to the combined group’s board.
Andy Briggs, Standard Life chief executive, said: “Our agreement to acquire Aegon UK significantly accelerates our vision to be the UK’s leading retirement savings and income business.
“Together, we will not only be stronger, we will be better.”
Standard Life is understood to have seen off rival bidders such as Lloyds Banking Group and Barclays to secure the deal.
Amsterdam-listed Aegon, which is based in Schiphol in the Netherlands, put its UK arm up for sale at the end of last year as part of a group-wide overhaul that will see it move its headquarters to the US and be renamed as Transamerica.
Standard Life said the deal – set to complete around the end of 2026 – will catapult it to second place in Britain’s retail pensions and savings market and in the same position for workplace pensions, adding Aegon UK’s 3.8 million customers and £160 billion in assets under management.
It is aiming to drive savings of £110 million a year after the deal, with over half delivered by the end of 2029 and the rest by the end of 2031, driven by cuts made across combined group and head office operations and as the pair integrate their platforms.
Lard Friese, Aegon chief executive, said: “The businesses are complementary and the combination offers an excellent outcome for Aegon UK’s customers and colleagues.
“Aegon’s shareholding will provide an opportunity to participate in the future success of the enlarged group.”
Phoenix Group bought Standard Life’s insurance business from the then Standard Life Aberdeen in 2018 and announced plans to rebrand as Standard Life last year.
It also has brands including SunLife, Phoenix Life, ReAssure and Phoenix Wealth.
Panmure Liberum analyst Abid Hussain said: “Overall, this looks like a good deal, although there will be questions on why the expense and capital synergies take five years to fully realise; we would ordinarily expect this to be achieved in three years.”

Standard Life buys Aegon's UK business for £2bn
Standard Life has agreed to buy the UK arm of Dutch insurer Aegon for £2billion, in a further bid to grow its share of the pensions market.
The FTSE 100 firm, formerly Phoenix Group, said the cash-and-share deal will create the country's largest pensions group, with 16 million customers and £480billion of assets under administration.
The deal will see Standard Life pay £750million in cash and issue 181.1million new shares to Aegon, meaning the Dutch insurer will hold a 15.3 per cent stake in the group.
Aegon announced in December that it was weighing a sale of its UK insurance business, which has more than 3.5 million customers, as part of its push into the US.
As part of the move, Aegon will relocate its headquarters to the US and rename itself Transamerica Inc.
Standard Life has come out on top in the battle for Aegon UK, after the Dutch insurer reportedly attracted interest from the Royal Bank of Canada, Lloyds and Royal London.
It is the latest sign of increased competition among pension providers looking to boost their customer bases and expand their offerings.
Chief executive Andy Briggs said: 'Our agreement to acquire Aegon UK significantly accelerates our vision to be the UK's leading retirement savings and income business. We will be in an even stronger position to meet the evolving needs of our 16 million customers
'Together, we will not only be stronger, we will be better - helping our customers achieve better outcomes and greater financial security in later life.
'I look forward to welcoming everyone at Aegon UK to Standard Life in due course and working together to capture the huge potential in front of us.'
Shares in Standard Life rose 1.4 per cent to 723.8p.
Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club said: 'The UK has an ageing population and big pension adequacy gap, with more than half of current savers expected to struggle financially unless they up contributions, which offers big opportunities ahead for Standard Life.'

Standard Life buys Aegon’s UK business in £2bn deal
Standard Life has bought Aegon UK creating the nation’s second largest retail pensions and savings platform by assets.

The £2bn deal adds £160bn of assets under administration creating an enlarged group with approximately £480bn of AUA.
While the addition of 3.8mn customers brings Standard Life’s total to 16mn customers.
The company’s announcement today (April 15) said the acquisition will transform adviser offering by “securing a proven platform”.
Andy Briggs, group CEO of Standard Life, said: “Our agreement to acquire Aegon UK significantly accelerates our vision to be the UK’s leading retirement savings and income business.
“With financial wellbeing at the heart of everything it does, Aegon UK’s values and culture are aligned with our own.
“Together, we will not only be stronger, we will be better — helping our customers achieve better outcomes and greater financial security in later life.
“I look forward to welcoming everyone at Aegon UK to Standard Life in due course and working together to capture the huge potential in front of us.”
The deal will be funded through a combination of cash, debt and shares in Standard Life, with Aegon becoming a strategic shareholder and asset management partner.
The purchase of Aegon will allow Standard Life to “increase the accessibility of off platform solutions” and increase accessibility for advisers.
Standard Life expects the deal will increase group operating cash generation by £160mn a year.
Lard Friese, Aegon CEO, added: “The businesses are complementary and the combination offers an excellent outcome for Aegon UK’s customers and colleagues.
“Aegon’s shareholding will provide an opportunity to participate in the future success of the enlarged group.”

Standard Life buys Aegon UK for £2bn
Deal comes as large insurers and asset managers compete more aggressively for UK pension assets
Standard Life has struck a deal to buy the UK arm of Dutch insurer Aegon for £2bn, as companies step up their race for British retirement assets.
The Netherlands-based Aegon said in December that it would consider putting its UK insurance business up for sale as part of a pivot to the US life insurance market, where Aegon also said it would move its head office.
Scottish Widows, Royal London and private equity firm CVC had also shown interest in the sale of Aegon UK, the FT previously reported.
Standard Life’s £2bn bid was far above that of runner-up Lloyds Banking Group, which made a final offer of £1.4bn, according to people familiar with the matter.
The transaction will be funded through a combination of cash, debt and shares in Standard Life — the recently rebranded Phoenix Group. Aegon would become a shareholder and asset management partner to Standard Life, the companies said.
Aegon UK had more than 4mn customers as of 2023, according to its website, and oversaw more than £124bn in assets as of last year. It offers pensions and investment services.
The deal comes as large insurers and asset managers compete more aggressively for UK pension assets. Apollo-backed insurer Athora and the insurance arm of Brookfield, the Canadian alternative assets giant, both announced deals last year to take over specialists in pension risk transfers, in which companies pay insurers to take on their financial obligations to retirees.
The £2bn price “looks very good”, said KBW analyst Michele Ballatore in a note, adding that the business had been sold at a value of about 14 times expected earnings. KBW had valued it at about £1.4bn, or about eight times earnings.
Ballatore said the deal was a “positive development” for the wider Aegon business, which would use the cash to reduce debt and buy back shares.
The deal comes as Standard Life separately holds talks with US private capital firms about an investment in its pension risk-transfer business that would help increase its share of that market in the UK.
BlackRock, Blackstone, Sixth Street, KKR and the asset management arm of Goldman Sachs had all at some point been involved in talks, the FT previously reported.
Standard Life chief executive Andy Briggs said the deal would help achieve its goal of becoming the UK’s leading retirement savings and income business.
“The transaction accelerates our shift to capital-light whilst strengthening our cash, capital and earnings position to create increased value for shareholders,” he added.

Aegon offloads 200-year-old UK business to Standard Life for £2bn
Deal will create pensions and savings group with 16 million customers and £480bn of assets, while Aegon focuses on US
The Dutch financial services group Aegon has struck a £2bn deal to sell off its almost 200-year-old UK arm to Standard Life, as part of a US push in which the group will be rebranded as Transamerica.
Standard Life, previously known as Phoenix Group, said the deal to buy Aegon UK would create a pensions and savings group with 16 million customers and £480bn of assets under administration.
Aegon put its UK business up for sale late last year, with companies including Barclays and Lloyds Banking Group named as possible bidders, as part of a wider restructuring that will result in its headquarters moving to the US and rebranding as Transamerica.
Aegon’s UK arm, which has 3.7 million customers, traces its roots back to Edinburgh in 1831, when it was founded as Scottish Equitable. Aegon acquired the business in 1998, rebranding as Aegon in the UK in 2009.
The FTSE 100 company Standard Life is paying £750m in cash for the business, and issuing 181.1m new shares to Aegon.
Lard Friese, the chief executive of Aegon, said: “The transaction represents an important step in our ambition to become a leading US life insurance and retirement group.
“Standard Life is the right owner for Aegon UK and a good home for our employees: we share the same values and a strong commitment to customers, and together the businesses will create the UK’s largest retirement savings and income provider.”
Aegon, which employs 2,000 staff in the UK with its headquarters in Edinburgh, will become the largest shareholder in Standard Life with a 15.3% stake. It will also be entitled to appoint one non-executive director to the group’s board.

Tracking Standard Life’s disjointed journey:
Is bigger better?
While for some years now, Phoenix — now Standard Life — would have been seen as a closed-book life fund consolidator, the acquisition of Aegon sets it on the path to become a growth-oriented retirement platform.
The deal creates the nation’s second-largest retail pensions and savings platform by assets. Standard Life boss Andy Briggs has said the deal significantly accelerates their vision to be the UK’s leading retirement savings and income business.
The £2bn deal adds £160bn of assets under administration, creating an enlarged group with approximately £480bn of AUA, while the addition of 3.8mn customers brings Standard Life’s total to 16mn customers.
Standard Life says the purchase of Aegon will allow it to “increase the accessibility of off-platform solutions” and increase accessibility for advisers.
Nouran Moustafa, practice principal and advisory strategy lead at Roxton Wealth, says on paper, the logic behind the deal is clear: the UK pensions and platform market is moving towards greater scale, regulation is becoming more demanding, and providers need the capital, technology and operational strength to support clients properly over the long term.
As a result, a deal of that size did not surprise her, but her immediate reaction to hearing about it was cautious optimism, with the emphasis very much on “cautious”.
Moustafa adds: “From an adviser’s perspective, scale is not automatically a client benefit. Advisers do not and should not judge platforms by the size of the balance sheet or the ambition in the press release.
“We judge them and should be judging by what happens when a client needs a transfer completed, a drawdown query resolved, a death claim handled sensitively, a platform error corrected, or a vulnerable client supported properly. That is where trust is either built or lost.”
Research by NextWealth has also found that advisers are tightening up platform panels at each review, looking across things like breadth of wrapper, data quality (as well as service).
“If taking the temperature, and based on our latest survey, which asked about willingness to recommend your platform, Aegon and Standard Life both rate below average.
“This will be important to the combined group to get in front of all of this sentiment, especially if a platform migration is on the horizon. Just because two large players have come together doesn’t automatically mean flows will be at the same rate.”
Napier notes there could also be some nervousness for those advisers affected by the post-acquisition problems in 2018, in the Cofunds to Aegon transaction.
Moustafa says following the Standard Life/Aegon deal announcement, she would neither recommend nor avoid a platform purely because of a merger announcement.
Her recommendations are based on client suitability, charges, functionality, financial strength, service, product features, investment options and the client’s specific needs.
However, during a major transition, she would naturally be more cautious before placing new business unless she had confidence that service standards, platform functionality and client communications were stable.
She says: “Pensions cannot tolerate uncertainty, and advisers have a duty to prioritise client protection over corporate momentum.”
According to Moustafa, while advisers are becoming more cautious when it comes to relying on large consolidated platforms, it does not mean they are anti-scale.
She says: “Scale can be valuable. It can fund better technology, stronger governance, improved investment capability and more robust retirement solutions.
“But advisers are increasingly aware that concentration can also reduce choice, make platforms feel less personal, and create a risk that service standards become too standardised for clients with more complex needs.
“The pensions market needs strong providers, but it also needs competition, innovation and genuine accountability. Bigger can be better, but only if it is also clearer, faster, more responsive and more client-focused.”
Integration frustration
Another big risk is how well the integration goes.
Nelson says this is significant because platform migrations and operating model changes are rarely painless.
And as such, advisers will be watching closely for signs that service standards are being protected (and improved); that the best people and capabilities from both businesses are retained; and that the combined group is investing in the adviser experience rather than simply extracting provider economics.
“So no, I don’t think this immediately makes Standard Life more attractive to the advice profession on day one. What it does do is give them the raw ingredients to become more attractive over time,” says Nelson.
“The question is whether they can turn scale, people, technology and a clearly defined strategy into something advisers actually feel in their day-to-day working lives.”
Platform migration has been a painful process for many organisations over an extended period of time.
However, according to Ian McKenna, founder of FTRC, it is important to recognise that Standard Life, as the recently rebranded Phoenix business, have a very long record of migrating legacy businesses: “Phoenix have done a huge amount behind the scenes in recent years to streamline their legacy systems. In this respect, I think Standard Life is probably one of the best homes for the Aegon book to move to.
“Historically, Aegon have had two main platforms, the old Cofunds platform and Aegon ARC (Aegon Retirement Choices). That said, Aegon also have a major workplace pension book.
“Like most platforms, some of their technology has been around for a long time, but there are also processes for continuous improvement.”
Additionally, moving to an organisation that has made investments in its underlying technology (Standard Life) over an extended period of years is better than staying with an institution (Aegon) that “is clearly no longer committed not just to the UK, but even Europe”, McKenna says.
However, he acknowledges that platform migration has historically been a painful process across the industry, even if Standard Life may be better placed than most to manage the transition - meaning execution will remain key.
A new strategy
A Standard Life spokesperson says Phoenix Group has shifted from consolidating closed-book life companies to a growth strategy following its acquisitions of Standard Life Assurance (2018) and the brand (2021).
This pivot focused first on pensions risk transfer and workplace pensions, generating £5.3bn in net workplace flows and £3.9bn in risk transfer deals last year.
The group now aims to become a top-five retail player, expanding its offering to individuals and advisers under the Standard Life brand, now reflected in its corporate name.
The proposed Aegon UK acquisition supports this strategy, strengthening its position in the retail intermediary market.
And by adding platform services to existing propositions, Standard Life expects to broaden adviser reach and enhance outcomes for clients: “Both businesses have made considerable investments in their services in recent years, and while we recognise the complexity of the task ahead, we believe there’s an opportunity to do more for advisers and their clients, and we are excited about the potential that the acquisition creates.”
Indeed, this deal gives Standard Life a very significant opportunity, but also a very significant responsibility.
The question is not whether the combined group becomes one of the biggest players in the market, but whether clients and advisers feel any meaningful improvement because of it.

Is this a good time to buy shares in Phoenix Group?
After changes in the budget to salary sacrifice pension contributions, this provider could prove resilient — despite a risk from US-based equities
While the stock market’s judgment is not infallible, there is more than meets the eye to the fact that shares in Phoenix Group have been at a consistently higher level since last week’s budget.
On the face of it the chancellor, Rachel Reeves, had bad news for Phoenix and other pension providers. She capped the national insurance contribution (NIC) relief on salary-sacrificed pension premiums at £2,000 per employee per year. Anything over that would now attract the same NIC tax as the rest of a worker’s pay.
This may discourage some higher paid staff from making those extra contributions, denying Phoenix profitable income. The chief executive, Andy Briggs, warned that it would make it harder for individuals to achieve financial security in retirement. And the increased administrative complexity for employers would do nothing to enhance the appeal of running these schemes.
But the impact on the Phoenix bottom line will be limited. The change will not take effect until April 2029, giving the pensions sector plenty of time to adapt. And pension contributions, including those of more than £2,000 a year, will still be free of income tax, so that incentive will remain.
As far as Phoenix shares are concerned, after the budget the salary sacrifice issue has been overshadowed by Reeves’s measures as a whole, which have been viewed in the City as non-inflationary and creating more fiscal headroom than expected. That has fuelled the belief that the Bank of England will continue cutting interest rates. The consequent rise in gilts (UK government bonds) has improved the value of Phoenix’s long-dated liabilities, a key factor in the value of its shares.
Such abstruse calculations are part and parcel of analysing this company, which began in its modern form 22 years ago, buying and managing undervalued life funds that had been closed to new business. After the low-hanging fruit had been snapped up and there were no longer so many funds to buy, the business evolved into a broad-based retirement savings and income business with four arms.
The first, pensions and savings, manages defined-contribution workplace pension schemes. The second, retirement solutions, handles defined-benefit schemes and annuities. Thirdly, with-profits manages legacy pensions and savings policies. Finally, Europe and “other” covers Ireland and Germany.
The seeds of radical change were sown seven years ago, when Phoenix bought the venerable Standard Life, which houses the first two divisions as the future growth engines. This will be formally recognised in March, when the group’s name will change from Phoenix to Standard Life. The legacy operations will provide a predictable and efficient cash stream to fund dividends and reinvestment.
The group is capitalising on a bulk purchase annuity boom arising from relatively high interest rates. That has improved pension scheme funding, leading to record demand for insurers to take over defined-benefit liabilities.
Regulatory reforms have helped. Britain’s shift to Solvency UK has reduced the required risk margin for long-term liabilities, releasing capital that Phoenix can deploy into new business or cutting debt. Analysts at Panmure Liberum predict that the gap between uncommitted cash and expected dividends will expand, throwing up a bonanza of excess cash by 2027.

And 60 per cent of the equities Phoenix manages are based in the United States, therefore exposed to a revaluation of technology shares.
